First off, you're gonna need gimp, which is free and an image that you want to make into a stencil. I'm also gonna assume that you're smart enough that I can give you all the important information and you can learn from your own creations.

As far as the image is concerned, it's better if the subject is pretty clear and apparent from the background. I find that with my method real life pictures sometimes work, but if you have a favorite anime or cartoon it's a lot better bet. Say for example that you want to make this image into a stencil.

First what you have to go into gimp, toss the image in and select threshold. I'm also going to assume, since you're probably smarter than the average bear, that you can find threshold in your version of gimp, since last I checked the default config for gimp was a clusterfuck.

Anyways, now you should be seeing something like this. Now this is the part where I was going to talk about how to not fuck up the threshold process, but with a simple image like this playing with the sliders is barely noticeable. I'm just gonna assume that you can fiddle with the values until you get whatever works for you, it's not like you can fuck up and not notice most of the time.

Now for the bridges, which is where you can really get into the time consuming part if you're doing a complex or multilayer stencil. I normally just print straight up and put in the bridges by hand with pencil or sharpie or something, but I'll do them here in red on the template itself and note why I put them there in the image.

Now the way that I do it, there are three reasons that I put a bridge somewhere, in no particular order and as marked on the image 1. Because if I were to cut it out it would flop around and possibly not stick to the piece I'm working on 2. Because it's an island and if I were to cut around it part of the stencil would fall out 3. Because it's a long straight line and I might risk having uneven line thickness or having the stencil wrinkle if I reinforce it. And the 4 is there to note that it's always better to bridge in corners instead of in the middle of lines, because it breaks up the image less and looks better.

And that's the basics of it. As far as making multilayer, or making larger templates, maybe I'll write a guide on it, but it's not that hard to figure out yourself now that you know the barebones basics.
